profile.campus: QTS Fayetteville campus, 13 buildings, approximately 6.2 million sq ft, along Highway 54 West between Veterans Parkway and Tyrone Road
profile.reading:
This is the southernmost of the four mapped QTS buildings and the one nearest Highway 54, about 0.26 miles from the campus gate address at 1435 Highway 54 West. It is also the most elongated, a bar of roughly 344 metres east to west by 99 metres deep covering about 21,000 square metres or near 226,000 square feet of ground. It entered OpenStreetMap on 29 January 2026 alongside its neighbour to the north, the first two of the campus to be traced. Nine of the thirteen buildings the city counts on this campus are still unmapped.

Nothing on this campus was carrying load as of mid 2026. County and press records agree that no building was operational, that construction was expected to continue into 2030, and that peak site activity reached something like 8,000 workers with two concrete plants and seven bridges under construction. Water use to date has been for concrete, dust suppression, truck washing, worker facilities and commissioning tests rather than cooling. That distinction became a public dispute. The county water system installed a meter during a change from its Beacon system to advanced metering infrastructure across roughly 33,000 accounts, believed it was being read electronically, and later found it never had been. A retroactive bill of about 147,000 dollars followed, one meter read accounting for roughly 100,000 of it. Reporting in July 2026 put a single meter at 20.6 million gallons since February 2024 and all thirteen campus meters at 109 million gallons combined. A May 2025 county letter that described two water lines installed without county knowledge or inspection was later retracted by the county as a metering artefact.

The county's published position is that QTS use runs under 1 percent of a system producing about 17.3 million gallons a day against a permitted 22.8 million, that construction water is billed at 6.46 dollars per 1,000 gallons, double retail, and that residential pressure is unaffected. QTS states the campus will run a closed loop cooling system once in service, with annual water use it compares to about four American households, in the range of 9,000 to 12,000 gallons a month. Both of those are forward looking. What the record actually shows at this building today is a foundation, a footprint and a construction water bill.

sources.title: QTS confirmed as behind 250MW data center mega-project in Fayetteville, Georgia
Blackstone Funds Complete Acquisition of QTS Realty Trust

profile.campus_note: One of 4 buildings OpenStreetMap contributors have mapped under this name in this locality, numbered west to east.
profile.capacity_note: The 6.2 million square feet the City of Fayetteville states is the campus total across thirteen buildings, not the floor area of this building, and no operator or government source publishes a floor area for any individual building here. The outline mapped for this building covers roughly 21,000 square metres of ground, about 226,000 square feet, measuring approximately 344 metres east to west by 99 metres deep, the most elongated of the four. That is a volunteer trace of a roof from aerial imagery, so it is a footprint and not a gross floor area, and the buildings in the approved programme were described as primarily two storey. It is the closest of the four mapped buildings to the campus gate address on Highway 54 West, about 0.26 miles away, and the only one for which that address is a close description. None of the four power fields carries a value on this row. There is no published IT load, so it_capacity_mw is absent and absence is the correct answer. There is no published utility service figure for this building, so utility_power_mw is absent, and the substation transformer rating recorded in campus_power_note is campus level apparent power rather than a building service. No standby diesel rating and no on site generation figure has been published either.
profile.facility_note: QTS Fayetteville, Georgia: a planned 600-acre, 250MW, 1.5M sq ft mega-campus, over $1 billion in expected investment, on land Facebook once considered before choosing Newton County.
profile.research_note:
Gap-view review: this is one of several rows tracking QTS's planned (not-yet-built) Fayette County, GA megacampus (600 acres, planned 250MW/1.5M sqft total per Data Center Dynamics 2022 reporting); no per-building figures exist for this pre-construction site, and no per-building breakout is published for however many buildings will comprise the eventual campus. No numeric key written.

[2026-09-05, Claude] Campus facts from the City of Fayetteville data centre FAQ. The city states one campus, thirteen buildings, approximately 6.2 million sq ft, on Highway 54 West between Veterans Parkway and Tyrone Road. Four buildings are mapped in OpenStreetMap and carry this shared campus record; the other nine are not mapped. No per-building floor area or IT capacity is published by QTS or the city, so none is stored. The prohibition on new data centres, Ordinance 26-O-12 of 5 March 2026, is recorded because it is a fact about the site regulatory setting, not a judgement about it.
profile.community_note: Fayetteville and Fayette County both answer residents in public, and the two records can be read against each other. The city publishes a data centre FAQ that cites the Congressional Research Service on what a data centre is and why it draws power, and the Georgia Public Service Commission on rates. The county published its own facts page on this campus after a water dispute became public, stating that QTS monthly use is under 1 percent of a system producing about 17.3 million gallons a day against a permitted 22.8 million, and that construction water is billed at 6.46 dollars per 1,000 gallons, double the standard retail rate. The Commission froze Georgia Power base rates through 2028 on 31 July 2025 and says it is working to keep new data centres from shifting costs onto residential customers. In January 2025 it approved a rule allowing minimum billing requirements and longer contract terms for new large load customers and requiring new data centre contracts to be filed with the Commission at least 30 days before signing. Residents near Old Hopeful Church and along Graves Road objected to the transmission route serving this campus during the second half of 2024.
profile.incentives_note: The city states that QTS project estimates put the campus at 150 million to 200 million dollars a year in real property tax revenue and about 170 million dollars in sales tax revenue, supporting several hundred ongoing operational jobs alongside construction and indirect employment. Those are operator estimates relayed by the city, not assessed collections, and they were published while no building on the campus was in service. An operator projection quoted by a city is still an operator projection. The county records a smaller but actually measured revenue stream from the same project during construction, in the region of 500,000 dollars a year in water sales at the doubled construction rate, with monthly bills of 35,000 to 38,000 dollars at peak activity.
profile.regulatory_note: No further data centre may be built in Fayetteville, and the prohibition has a traceable origin. On 27 January 2026 the city planning and zoning commission denied a conceptual site plan for a data centre proposed by Crow Holdings Development on Highway 85 North beyond the Fayette Pavilion shopping centre. The council then imposed a 90 day moratorium on data centre applications while it rewrote the code, and the city attorney Patrick Jaugstetter confirmed at the January work session that the council could advertise an extension if the rewrite ran long. City manager Ray Gibson told the council that the reason the use had not simply been struck from the ordinance earlier was the pending QTS expansion. On 5 March 2026 the council adopted Ordinance 26-O-12, amending chapters 200 and 400 of the Unified Development Ordinance to prohibit data centres in every zoning district in the city. Crow Holdings and CHI Acquisitions withdrew their appeal on 18 March 2026, the day before the council was to hear it, leaving the commission denial in place. The QTS campus was annexed, rezoned and site planned in 2022 and 2023 and is unaffected. Fayetteville now hosts roughly 6.2 million square feet of data centre and permits none.
profile.planned_capacity: Planned project: could extend to 250 MW and 1.5 million sq ft at full build-out on 600 acres (per Data Center Dynamics trade press); this is planned/future capacity, not confirmed current operating capacity, and is a project total not a per-building figure.
profile.regional_context: QTS was founded 2003, HQ Overland Park KS, acquired by Blackstone for ~$10B in 2021.
profile.campus_power_note: Electric service to the campus is from Georgia Power. The Development of Regional Impact plans filed for the site in January 2023 show five 150 MVA transformers stepping 230 kV down to 34.5 kV on site. That is substation transformer capacity in apparent power for the whole campus. It is not an IT load figure, not a per building service figure, and not a statement of what any one building will draw. Georgia Power has built two substations for the campus, named Charles and Creola, and a transmission line tying new customer substations to its Ashley Park substation, with completion expected in summer 2026. Residents near Old Hopeful Church and along Graves Road objected during the second half of 2024, some to the route and some to the project, and asked for rerouting or for the line to be buried. No operator statement, utility filing or local government record gives an IT load in megawatts for this campus or for any building on it, so no it_capacity_mw is recorded on any of the four rows. Trade coverage of the 2022 land purchase described a design target of about 250 MW for the original 615 acre programme. That is a design intention for a project, not a contracted service, not a measured load and not a building figure.
profile.facility_type_note: Part of QTS's Atlanta area footprint, which spans Atlanta proper, Fayette County and Gwinnett County, Georgia. This campus is the company's Fayetteville site, referred to in its own regional impact filings as ATL2, with the adjoining expansion filed as ATL2 East by QTS Eastwood, LLC in January 2026.

reading.body:
QTS acquired 600 acres in Fayette County, Georgia, roughly 20 miles south of Atlanta, in 2022 for $153.8 million. The company has announced a planned campus of 250 MW capacity across 1.5 million square feet of building space, with expected total investment exceeding $1 billion. The campus is designed as a 13-building project, though no per-building capacity figures are published and construction has not reached the phase where building-level specifications are confirmed.

No operating capacity at this campus is published. The campus remains in the planned or early acquisition phase, not yet generating measurable IT load. Until buildings become operational and their power draw is measured or disclosed, this site contributes zero megawatts to Georgia's current data center footprint or the grid's binding constraint on AI scaling.

If built to specification, the Fayetteville campus would rank as Georgia's largest published data center project by a substantial margin. Georgia Power has flagged data center load growth as a major driver of future generation and transmission investment in its regulatory filings. The state currently shows 66.3 megawatts of published capacity across four facilities with confirmed figures; this 250 MW project would represent a more than threefold increase in announced AI-accessible capacity.
